notes:
Task and constraints: Count words that can be stretched to match S by expanding runs of repeated characters.
Idea: Run-length encode S and each word, then compare run characters and lengths.
Technique and why it applies: The run-character sequences must match. Each target run must either equal the word run or have length at least three and be longer than the word run.
Invariant: R and count represent the target's run characters and lengths; R2/count2 represent one candidate word.
Edge cases: itertools.groupby handles adjacent runs. The code assumes S is nonempty because it unpacks RLE(S) into two values.
Complexity: Encoding and checking each word are linear in total input characters, with O(n) temporary run storage.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the first player wins the chalkboard XOR game.
Idea: Return True if the XOR of all numbers is zero or if the number of entries is even.
Technique and why it applies: The game-theoretic result says zero XOR is an immediate winning condition, and an even number of entries guarantees a winning strategy under optimal play.
Invariant: The reduction computes the XOR of every array element before applying the parity test.
Edge cases: The snippet uses functools.reduce and operator.xor without importing either module, so it fails unless these names are supplied externally.
Complexity: XOR reduction is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Check whether the first player has a winning strategy in the chalkboard XOR game.
Idea: Reduce the array by XOR and test whether the result is zero or the array length is even.
Technique and why it applies: The known strategy criterion for this game depends only on the initial XOR and parity of the number of values, not on simulating turns.
Invariant: reduce(xor, nums) is the XOR of all entries.
Edge cases: The code assumes nums is nonempty because reduce has no initializer. The standard problem constraints provide at least one number.
Complexity: One reduction takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count visits to each domain and all of its parent subdomains.
Idea: Split each count-domain entry into its visit count and domain labels, then build every suffix domain and accumulate its count.
Technique and why it applies: For a.b.c, the code adds the count to c, b.c, and a.b.c by traversing labels in reverse.
Invariant: output maps each full or parent domain to the sum of visits contributed by input entries.
Edge cases: The method prints intermediate subdomain lists and strings as debug output. It assumes each entry has a count followed by a domain separated by one space.
Complexity: Processing is O(total domain-label characters) time and O(U) map space for U distinct subdomains.

Task and constraints: Return visit counts for every domain and each of its subdomains.
Idea: Split each domain into labels and accumulate its count for every suffix.
Technique and why it applies: Reversing the label list and joining prefixes builds the full domain, its parent, and each higher-level suffix. A defaultdict sums visits across input lines.
Invariant: result[domain] is the total visits recorded for that exact domain.
Edge cases: split() tolerates multiple spaces between the count and domain. Output order follows dictionary insertion order and is not required to be sorted.
Complexity: Total parsing and aggregation are linear in input text length, with O(U) auxiliary map space.

Task and constraints: Find the largest area of any triangle formed by three input points.
Idea: Enumerate every triple and compute its area using the shoelace determinant.
Technique and why it applies: The absolute determinant of the coordinate differences gives twice the triangle area; multiplying by one half yields the area. The maximum over all triples is retained.
Invariant: maxA is the largest triangle area found among triples already examined.
Edge cases: Collinear triples contribute zero. combinations avoids duplicate point choices and uses each triple once.
Complexity: There are O(n³) triples, each with constant arithmetic, so time is O(n³) and auxiliary space O(1) beyond the combination iterator.

Task and constraints: Compute the largest triangle area from the supplied coordinate points.
Idea: Check every ordered-by-index triple and maximize the absolute shoelace formula.
Technique and why it applies: The determinant formula gives twice the area, so its absolute value is multiplied by 0.5. Iterating i<j<k avoids duplicate triples.
Invariant: result stores the largest area found over all triples processed so far.
Edge cases: Collinear points yield zero area. The code assumes at least three points for a nonzero candidate, though fewer points would return zero.
Complexity: The three nested loops give O(n³) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Partition an array into at most k groups to maximize the sum of each group's average.
Idea: Initialize each suffix as one group, then iteratively allow additional cuts using dynamic programming.
Technique and why it applies: dp[i] starts as the average of A[i:]. For each additional group allowance, the code tries every first-group endpoint j and combines that segment's average with dp[j+1].
Invariant: After each outer iteration, dp[i] is the best average sum for the suffix beginning at i using the current maximum number of groups.
Edge cases: The code assumes A is nonempty and k is positive. It shadows Python's built-in sum with a local variable, which does not affect this calculation.
Complexity: The nested loops and repeated segment sums take O(kn²) time and O(n) DP space.

Task and constraints: Find the number of buses needed to travel from source to target through routes, or return -1.
Idea: Build a stop-to-route graph and BFS over reachable stops, counting one bus each time a route is boarded.
Technique and why it applies: Each stop lists the bus routes serving it. Once a bus is first visited, all its stops are explored and marked; BFS layers correspond to number of buses taken.
Invariant: seen_stops contains stops already enqueued, and seen_buses prevents re-exploring the same route.
Edge cases: source==target returns zero. defaultdict and deque are imported inside the class body, but the method references them as unqualified globals, so this can raise NameError.
Complexity: Each route and stop is processed a bounded number of times, giving O(total route stops) time and space.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum buses needed to get from S to T.
Idea: BFS by bus count, using a map from each stop to routes that serve it.
Technique and why it applies: Each layer represents one more bus ride. When a route is used, its stops are explored and the route is removed from those stops to avoid processing the same route repeatedly.
Invariant: lookup contains stops already discovered, and result is the number of buses used to reach the current layer.
Edge cases: S==T returns zero. If T is unreachable, the queue empties and the method returns -1.
Complexity: Each route-stop incidence is processed at most a small number of times, so time and space are O(total route stops).

Task and constraints: Generate all valid coordinate interpretations of a digit string enclosed in parentheses.
Idea: Split the digits into left and right parts and generate legal integer or decimal forms for each side.
Technique and why it applies: A multi-digit integer cannot start with zero, and a fractional part cannot end in zero. The Cartesian product combines all valid representations of each split.
Invariant: _splitToNums returns all legal numeric forms for one digit substring.
Edge cases: The regex in _isValidSplit is written with slash delimiters, which Python regex does not treat as anchors; it therefore does not perform the intended all-zero test. The code also lacks imports for re and itertools.
Complexity: The number of splits and representations can grow quadratically in digit length; output size dominates time and space.

Task and constraints: Return all valid decimal coordinate pairs represented by the digits inside S's outer parentheses.
Idea: Enumerate every split point and generate valid integer/decimal forms for both substrings.
Technique and why it applies: A side may be an integer or a decimal, but multi-digit integers cannot start with zero and fractional parts cannot end in zero. itertools.product combines each valid left and right form.
Invariant: make(S,i,n) yields all valid numeric interpretations of a fixed digit segment.
Edge cases: Single zero is allowed; leading zeros in longer integer parts and trailing zeros in fractional parts are rejected. The input is assumed to have enclosing parentheses.
Complexity: Enumerating splits and candidate forms can produce O(n²) output candidates, with time and space proportional to the generated results.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum instructions for a race car to reach target position, starting at position zero with speed one.
Idea: Use BFS over (position,speed) states, exploring accelerate and reverse actions.
Technique and why it applies: Accelerate moves to pos+speed and doubles speed; reverse leaves position unchanged and changes speed to ±1. BFS returns the first target state in increasing instruction count.
Invariant: Every state in the current queue layer is reachable in exactly steps instructions.
Edge cases: The code uses pop(0), which shifts the remaining list and is slower than deque.popleft. The reverse condition is a pruning heuristic tied to crossing the target.
Complexity: The state space is large and BFS can be exponential in target magnitude; queue operations with list front removal add linear overhead.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum sequence of accelerate and reverse instructions that reaches target.
Idea: Use dynamic programming over target positions, considering a full run of accelerations and overshoot/undershoot strategies.
Technique and why it applies: k=bit_length gives the acceleration count near target. Exact all-accelerate positions use k steps; other cases consider overshooting and reversing, or undershooting then reversing twice.
Invariant: dp[i] is the minimum instruction count to reach position i from the start.
Edge cases: Target is positive under the problem constraints. The inner recurrence indexes positions derived from smaller bit patterns and relies on already computed DP entries.
Complexity: For each i, up to O(log i) alternatives are checked, giving O(target log target) time and O(target) space.

Task and constraints: Return the most common word in a paragraph excluding banned words.
Idea: Normalize punctuation and case, split into words, count frequencies, and remove banned entries.
Technique and why it applies: Translating punctuation to spaces prevents punctuation from joining words; lowercasing makes matching case-insensitive. Counter.most_common selects the highest-frequency remaining word.
Invariant: para_count holds frequencies of normalized paragraph words not removed by the banned list.
Edge cases: The code imports string and Counter inside the class body, but references them unqualified inside the method; this may raise NameError unless imported globally. It assumes at least one non-banned word remains.
Complexity: Text normalization and counting take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the most frequent non-banned word in paragraph, ignoring case and common punctuation.
Idea: Lowercase and split the paragraph, count tokens, then select the highest-frequency token not in banned.
Technique and why it applies: Counter records frequencies, and the loop updates result only when a non-banned word has a strictly higher count than the current choice.
Invariant: result is the most frequent eligible word among tokens processed so far.
Edge cases: The strip call removes punctuation only from token ends and omits some punctuation characters such as semicolon, so embedded or unlisted punctuation may remain attached to words. It assumes a valid answer exists.
Complexity: Tokenization/counting and selection are O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum length of a reference string that encodes all words as suffixes ending with #.
Idea: Build a reverse trie of unique words and count the lengths of words whose terminal trie nodes are leaves.
Technique and why it applies: Reversing each word makes suffix relationships become prefixes. If a word ends at a leaf, no longer word contains it as a suffix, so it needs its own encoded segment.
Invariant: trie_root stores reversed word paths, and tail_nodes stores each word's terminal node and length plus delimiter.
Edge cases: Duplicate words are removed before insertion. A word that is a suffix of another ends at an internal node and contributes no separate encoding length.
Complexity: Trie construction is O(total characters) expected time and space.

Task and constraints: Compute the shortest reference encoding of a word list, allowing words that are suffixes of others to share storage.
Idea: Insert reversed unique words into a trie and sum length plus one for each word ending at a leaf.
Technique and why it applies: A suffix word's reversed path is a prefix of a longer reversed word, so its terminal node is not a leaf and it needs no separate encoding.
Invariant: nodes[i] points to the trie node reached by the reversed word words[i].
Edge cases: Duplicate words are removed before building the trie. Empty words are outside the usual constraints.
Complexity: Trie construction is O(total characters) expected time and space; the final leaf scan is O(number of unique words).

Task and constraints: For each position in s, return the distance to the nearest occurrence of character c.
Idea: Collect every index containing c, then compare each position with all such indices.
Technique and why it applies: The minimum absolute index difference is the shortest distance along the string to an occurrence of c.
Invariant: ch stores all occurrence positions of c, and min_d is reset for each source position before checking candidates.
Edge cases: The code assumes c occurs in s; otherwise every position returns len(s). Empty s returns an empty list.
Complexity: If n is string length and m is the number of c occurrences, time is O(nm) and auxiliary storage is O(n+m).

Task and constraints: Compute each character's distance to the nearest occurrence of C.
Idea: Make a forward pass to account for previous occurrences and a backward pass to account for next occurrences.
Technique and why it applies: prev stores the nearest occurrence encountered in the current direction. Each pass lowers result[i] to the distance from that occurrence, and the minimum of both directions is the answer.
Invariant: After the forward scan, result stores distances to nearest left occurrences where available; the reverse scan adds right-side candidates.
Edge cases: The initial prev=-len(S) acts as a large distance before any occurrence. The problem guarantees C appears in S.
Complexity: Two passes take O(n) time and O(n) result space.
